newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Fed seen looking past April jobs gains.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Fed seen looking past April jobs gains.

text.p: The April U.S. employment report, due Friday, will likely show continued job and wage growth but fall shy of convincing Federal Reserve officials to tighten monetary policy at their May 20 meeting, analysts said on Wednesday.
"A strong employment report could have an impact, but it's not going to completely round out any arguments," said Matt Alexy, chief markets strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.

The spotlight will fall on the overall unemployment figure, expected to hold steady at 5.2 percent, while of secondary importance will be the headline payrolls figure, seen rising 211,000 from a 175,000 gain in March.

"Any further decline in the unemployment rate would probably increase the likelihood of tightening of monetary policy, even though inflation is pretty good," said David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.

The Fed will likely wait until the April retail sales report on May 13 before finalizing any policy decisions. Policy makers pointed to the underlying strength in consumer demand as the main force prompting the 25-basis point federal funds rate rise in March.

"If it comes in line with my expectations, I think it will make for a very close call in the May Fed meeting," said Resler, who forcast a 190,000 gain in April payrolls and an unemployment rate of 5.3 percent.
"In fact, it will probably shift the focus entirely to things like retail sales," he added.
Wayne Ayers, chief economist at the Bank of Boston, said what the Fed needs to see is "any indication final demand will be softening or not".
Recently, Federal Reserve officials have said the current relatively low unemployment rate means the economy is operating above its long-run capacity.
Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer warned last week that the U.S. "economy appears to be growing at an unsustainable, above-trend rate".

Tuesday's surprisingly weak Employment Cost Index (ECI) stole the thunder from the average hourly earnings component, which was expected to have risen 0.3 percent in April after gaining 0.4 percent in March.

The ECI, which is considered a more comprehensive measure than average hourly earnings because it includes both wages and compensation, rose 0.6 percent in the first quarter of 1997, much lower than the 0.9 percent rise expected by Wall Street.

Following Wednesday's release of a sharp 5.6 percent jump in first quarter gross domestic product, markets will anxiously eye the April employment report as it provides the first glimpse of second quarter economic performance.
"The GDP numbers came in strong, so what the market is going to be looking for now is some indication of whether or not momentum is carried forward into the second quarter," Ayers said.
However, the payrolls report will only shed light on the production, not demand, side of the equation, analysts said.
The data will be released at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
